stem: A team trains a model by running 30 passes over the same 200 GB dataset. Their earlier MapReduce implementation wrote every pass's output to distributed storage and read it back at the start of the next pass. Which Apache Spark capability most directly cuts the run time of the iterative job?

choices.text: Spark compresses all intermediate data with a lossy codec, so each pass reads far fewer bytes than the original dataset holds.
Spark fuses all 30 passes into a single task automatically, so the dataset is scanned only once regardless of how many actions run.
Spark replaces the cluster manager with a built-in single JVM scheduler, so no resources have to be negotiated before each pass starts.
Spark can keep the working dataset in executor memory across passes with `cache()` or `persist()`, so later passes skip the re-read from storage.

stem: A company runs nightly SQL ETL, a streaming ingestion job and a model-training job on three separate systems, each with its own API, optimizer and cluster. Which benefit of adopting Apache Spark addresses this fragmentation?

choices.text: Spark ships its own distributed file system, so ETL, streaming and training jobs no longer need an external storage layer for their data.
One engine with shared DataFrame and SQL APIs covers batch, streaming and machine learning, so one optimizer and one cluster serve all three workloads.
Spark rewrites any pipeline into a single-node program, which removes network transfer and the need to size a cluster for each workload.
Spark converts streaming and machine-learning code to plain SQL automatically, so developers no longer need to learn any module-specific API.

stem: A nightly job reads a folder of 3 million JSON files of about 50 KB each (150 GB total). A Spark UI check shows that the read stage takes longer than the whole transformation that follows, although the cluster has idle cores. Which Spark challenge does this describe?

choices.text: Too many executors are registered, so the driver spends the stage time rebalancing cached blocks between them.
Lazy evaluation is recomputing the folder listing once for every column used later in the query plan.
The small-files problem: opening and listing millions of tiny files adds per-file overhead that dwarfs the data scanned.
A wide transformation is moving data across the network, which is the cost of a shuffle rather than of the file read.

stem: A node in a Spark cluster fails in the middle of a long batch job, and the partitions it held are lost. Which Spark characteristic lets the job finish without the developer having to restart it by hand?

choices.text: Spark records the lineage of transformations behind each partition and recomputes only the lost partitions on other executors.
The driver writes a full checkpoint to distributed storage after every transformation, so work always resumes from the last step.
The cluster manager pauses the application until the failed node returns and then replays the stage on that same node.
Every partition is automatically replicated to three nodes before any transformation runs, so a copy is always available elsewhere.

stem: A developer's job runs `orderBy` on a 2 TB DataFrame and then `groupBy("country").count()` on the result. The Spark UI shows heavy "Shuffle Read" and "Shuffle Write" and long stage times compared with a plain `filter` pass over the same data. What is the underlying challenge?

choices.text: Wide transformations must redistribute rows across executors over the network and through disk, which costs far more than narrow, per-partition work.
Narrow transformations such as `filter` are always slower than `groupBy` because they are executed by the driver one partition at a time.
Each `orderBy` and `groupBy` forces Spark to collect the full 2 TB onto the driver, which then redistributes the result back to the executors.
The data is stored in columnar format, which prevents Spark from running sorts and aggregations in parallel on more than one core.

stem: A developer wants to look at a sample of a 90 GB DataFrame `big_df` as Python objects on a driver with 8 GB of memory. Which call keeps the amount of data brought to the driver bounded?

choices.text: `big_df.collect()`, because the result is returned in batches so the driver never holds more than one partition at a time.
`big_df.rdd.collect()`, because the RDD API streams rows to the driver lazily and releases them after each use.
`big_df.toPandas()`, because the Arrow conversion compresses the rows so the 90 GB fits into the 8 GB driver heap.
`big_df.limit(20).collect()`, because only the 20 requested rows are sent from the executors to the driver.

stem: Two engineers implement the same aggregation in PySpark. One uses `df.groupBy("k").agg(F.sum("v"))`; the other uses a Python lambda on an RDD from `df.rdd.map(...).reduceByKey(...)`. The DataFrame version runs noticeably faster on the same cluster. Which advantage of Spark's structured APIs explains it?

choices.text: The RDD version cannot run in parallel because Python lambdas hold the global interpreter lock on the whole cluster at once.
DataFrame operations are planned by the Catalyst optimizer and executed by the JVM engine, so Python code does not touch each row.
DataFrames keep all data on disk in a compressed format, so they never need the memory that RDD lambdas consume.
DataFrame code runs only on the driver, so it avoids the cost of shipping work to executors that the lambda version pays.

stem: A PySpark application is launched with `spark-submit`. It reads a Parquet table, transforms it and writes the result. Which component builds the execution plan for the application, splits each job into stages and tasks, and sends those tasks to executors?

choices.text: The cluster manager, which examines the code of the application to build its stages before any executor is started.
Each executor, by negotiating with the other executors in the cluster to share the stages of every job.
The driver, whose SparkSession and scheduler turn the DataFrame operations into stages and tasks for the executors.
The worker node's operating system, which turns each DataFrame operation into tasks for the local cores.

stem: An administrator wants to understand which Spark component decides how many executor processes, and with how many cores and how much memory, are started for an application on a shared YARN or Kubernetes cluster. Which component grants these resources?

choices.text: The block manager on each executor, which reserves memory on peers when a cached partition does not fit.
The cluster manager, which allocates resources across applications and launches the executors Spark asks for.
The Spark SQL catalog, which stores per-table settings for executor sizing and applies them at query time.
The driver's task scheduler, which chooses the number of cores each executor uses after tasks are submitted.

stem: An executor is started with a 10 GB heap, and the unified memory region M is shared by execution (shuffles, joins, sorts) and storage (cached blocks). Which setting defines the part of M whose cached blocks execution is not allowed to evict?

choices.text: `spark.executor.memoryOverhead`, which reserves memory for cached blocks outside the JVM heap.
`spark.memory.fraction`, which sets the share of the heap that cached blocks may never leave.
`spark.memory.storageFraction`, which sets the subregion R of M where cached blocks are immune to eviction.
`spark.driver.maxResultSize`, which limits how much cached data an executor may hold in memory.

stem: A cluster has 3 executors, each with 4 cores, and `spark.task.cpus` is 1. A stage has 60 tasks that each take about 10 seconds and the cluster runs nothing else. Ignoring scheduling overhead, roughly how long does the stage take?

choices.text: About 50 seconds, because 12 tasks run at once and the 60 tasks need five waves.
About 10 seconds, because Spark starts all 60 tasks at the same moment.
About 600 seconds, because tasks of a single stage must run one after another.
About 150 seconds, because only one executor's 4 cores can run tasks at a time.

stem: A long-running application loses one of its executors to a node failure while a cached DataFrame is spread across all executors. The driver is healthy. What happens?

choices.text: The driver restarts every stage of the application from the first job onward, discarding all of the results computed so far.
The cluster manager restores the lost partitions from a hidden replica and the same task resumes from its last point on a new node.
The application fails at once, because cached data lost together with an executor cannot be rebuilt after the original job has started.
Spark reschedules the lost executor's tasks elsewhere and recomputes the lost cached partitions from lineage when they are next needed.

stem: Two data scientists each run a notebook that is its own Spark application on the same cluster. The first reads a large table and calls `cache()` followed by `count()`. The second then reads the same table and runs a query. What does the second application see?

choices.text: The second application reads from storage again, because each application has its own executors and cached data is not shared between applications.
The second application can attach to the cached DataFrame once the first one's driver is told to broadcast it.
The second application reads the cached blocks only if it uses the same `appName` as the first one.
Both applications share one block store on the cluster, so the second notebook reads the first notebook's cached partitions.

stem: A developer runs the code below on a cluster and notices that the `print` output from the `foreach` call does not appear in the notebook or driver console, while the `total` line prints normally. ``` rows = df.filter("x > 5").collect() total = sum(r.x for r in rows) print(total) df.foreach(lambda r: print(r.x)) ``` Where does each part run?

choices.text: The `sum` runs on the cluster manager, and the `foreach` lambda runs on the driver after the stage completes.
Both run on executors, and Spark forwards the first `print` to the driver console but drops the one inside `foreach`.
Both run in the driver, but `foreach` output is buffered until the driver finishes and is then written to the console on exit.
The `sum` runs in the driver's Python process after `collect`, and the `foreach` lambda runs on executors, so its prints go to the executor logs.

stem: A Scala developer moves to PySpark and asks which structured abstraction replaces the typed `Dataset[T]` API in Python. Which statement is accurate?

choices.text: PySpark's DataFrame runs on a separate Python engine and supports only a subset of the optimizations of the Scala DataFrame.
The typed `Dataset[T]` API exists only in Scala and Java; Python uses the untyped DataFrame, which runs on the same Catalyst engine.
PySpark provides the typed `Dataset[T]` API through a Python decorator, which gives compile-time type checking of column types.
PySpark exposes only RDDs to developers, because DataFrames and Datasets exist only in the Scala and Java languages.

stem: A notebook cell builds a SparkSession and then a second cell, run later, executes the same builder call with a different `appName`. ``` s1 = SparkSession.builder.appName("etl").getOrCreate() s2 = SparkSession.builder.appName("report").getOrCreate() ``` What does the second call do?

choices.text: It creates a second independent SparkContext and session, so the application now runs two separate sets of executors.
It raises an error because only one session may be built per Python process, and the builder refuses a second call.
It returns the existing session instead of creating another, because `getOrCreate()` reuses the active global default session.
It stops the first session and builds a new one, which discards the first session's cached tables and temporary views.

stem: A developer runs the code below and wants to know what happens on each line with respect to caching. ``` df = spark.read.parquet(path).filter("amount > 0").cache() n = df.count() s = df.agg({"amount": "sum"}).first() ``` Which description is correct?

choices.text: Nothing is cached, because `cache()` only has an effect on RDDs and ignores DataFrames in PySpark.
`cache()` only marks the plan; `count()` materializes the cached partitions, and the aggregation later reads them from cache.
`cache()` loads the data into memory at once, so `count()` and the aggregation both read the cached copy without any scan.
Both actions rescan the Parquet files because `cache()` stores data only for the lifetime of the single action that called it.

stem: A 25 GB DataFrame read through JDBC is reused by many later actions. The executors have about 10 GB of storage memory in total, and re-reading from the source database is slow and expensive. Which choice best fits?

choices.text: `persist(StorageLevel.MEMORY_ONLY)`, so partitions that do not fit in memory are recomputed from the JDBC source each time they are needed.
`persist(StorageLevel.DISK_ONLY)`, because any cached data should stay off executor memory to leave all memory for execution.
`persist(StorageLevel.MEMORY_AND_DISK)`, so partitions that do not fit in memory are written to local disk and read back instead of recomputed.
`persist(StorageLevel.MEMORY_AND_DISK_2)`, because replicating every partition is the only way to keep the cached data complete.

stem: A loop builds a new cached DataFrame on each of 50 iterations, and each iteration uses only its own cached result. After about 20 iterations stages slow down, and the Storage tab shows that executor storage memory is full of old iterations' blocks. Which fix targets the cause?

choices.text: Call `cache()` a second time on each new DataFrame, so Spark prioritizes it over the older cached blocks.
Call `spark.catalog.clearCache()` at the start of each iteration, even though some cached tables are still used later.
Call `checkpoint()` on every iteration, because checkpointing removes older cached blocks from executor memory.
Call `unpersist()` on the previous iteration's DataFrame once the new one is materialized, so its blocks are released.

stem: A job caches several large DataFrames. In the Spark UI the tasks show long garbage collection times, and the GC log on the executors shows the Old generation almost full. Which adjustment does the Spark tuning guide suggest first for this symptom?

choices.text: Lower `spark.memory.fraction`, so less memory is used for cached objects and the Old generation is not full.
Cache with a `_2` replicated storage level, so a second copy on another node absorbs the pressure of collections.
Raise `spark.memory.fraction` toward 0.9, so Spark can cache more objects before collections are needed.
Increase `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` to 2000, since a larger number of shuffle partitions empties the Old generation.

stem: A developer runs the following in a notebook where `spark` is an existing session. ``` s2 = spark.newSession() spark.range(3).createOrReplaceTempView("t") s2.sql("SELECT * FROM t").show() ``` What happens on the last line?

choices.text: It fails because `newSession()` starts a new application with its own executors, which cannot read the first session's data.
It prints the three rows, because `newSession()` copies the registered views of the original session.
It prints the three rows, because temporary views are shared by every session that runs on the same SparkContext.
It fails because `t` is not found: temporary views are session-scoped, although the new session shares the SparkContext and table cache.

stem: A developer runs the code below on a new session. Which lines cause Spark to start a job? ``` df = spark.range(1_000_000) a = df.filter("id % 2 = 0") b = a.withColumn("sq", a.id * a.id) n = b.count() b.write.mode("overwrite").parquet(out) ```

choices.text: Only the `count()` and `write` lines; the lines that build `df`, `a` and `b` only add transformations to the plan.
Only the `write` line, since `count()` can be answered from metadata and does not need a job.
Every line, because each statement creates a new DataFrame that Spark computes immediately.
The `filter` and `withColumn` lines, because transformations run when defined and actions only fetch the result.

stem: A developer reads a Parquet table and chains `filter`, `withColumn`, `coalesce(4)` and `groupBy("k").count()` before writing. Which of these transformations forces Spark to create a new stage because it needs a shuffle?

choices.text: `filter`, since it must inspect every row of the table and so needs the rows redistributed between executors first.
`withColumn`, since adding a new column forces all existing data to be moved so that every partition has it.
`groupBy("k").count()`, since rows with the same key must be brought together in one partition.
`coalesce(4)`, since it always shuffles all rows to reduce the partition count.

stem: A developer creates a DataFrame with `spark.range(0, 1000, 1, 8)`, which has 8 partitions, applies `filter` and `select`, and then calls `count()`. In the Spark UI, how many tasks does the first stage of that job run?

choices.text: 1000, because a stage runs one task for each row.
8, because a stage runs one task for each partition of its input.
1, because a stage runs one task for each job.
200, because every stage uses `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` tasks.

stem: One task in a stage fails with a transient exception, for example a brief connection reset to an external database. Assume default Spark settings. What does Spark do?

choices.text: It aborts the job immediately, because any single failed task means that the stage result would be incomplete and unusable.
It retries the task, possibly on another executor, and aborts the job only if the task fails `spark.task.maxFailures` times (default 4).
It reruns every task of the whole stage from the start and throws away the output of tasks that had already succeeded.
It skips that partition and continues, so the job finishes with a result that is missing the failed task's rows.

stem: A developer runs `agg = df.groupBy("k").count()` and calls `agg.count()` and then `agg.show()`, with no `cache()` anywhere. In the Spark UI the second job lists a stage as "skipped". What explains this?

choices.text: The skipped stage's tasks were automatically replicated to another executor, so they need not run again.
The second job was partly cancelled by the driver because the first job already returned the same data to the application.
The shuffle output files written by the first job are still available, so Spark reuses them and skips recomputing that stage.
Adaptive Query Execution removed the stage because the aggregation contained no rows to process.

stem: Which ordering lists Spark execution units from the smallest to the largest?

choices.text: Task, stage, job, application
Job, stage, task, application
Task, job, stage, application
Stage, task, job, application
